Most other facts are accurate and well woven in, including cuju, the Freemasons' Tavern, hacking and rugby, the ball-per-half final, Gaetjens, Pickles, Ken Aston's cards, the Dick, Kerr Ladies, Chastain and Messi. The 'thought there must have been a typo' newspaper story is a popular legend and is not hedged.

story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Duck Who Remembered Bricks
story.subtitle: A sleepy trip back to where LEGO began

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Wooden Duck Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Milo stacked red bricks into a tower. Juno stomped a toy dinosaur beside it.

A toy shark watched from the rug. It was way past bedtime. The boys should be asleep.

Milo pressed one more brick. CLICK! The tower wiggled. It did not fall.

Then something glowed in the toy box. A little wooden duck blinked its eyes.

"Quack-quack-CLACK!" it said. "I am Clack. I am the oldest toy in this whole room."

Juno gasped. "A talking duck!"

Clack waddled onto the rug, wobbling on his little wooden feet. "Want to see where bricks began?" he asked.

Milo grinned. "Yes! Yes please!"

Clack tapped his wooden wing. The rug turned soft and swirly, like water.

WHOOOSH! The boys landed in a sunny yard. Wood shavings covered the ground like curly snow.

A man sat carving a little wooden duck, just like Clack.

"That's Ole Kirk," said Clack. "He's a carpenter. That means he makes things out of wood."

"Hello, boys," said Ole Kirk. "Want to help me carve?"

Milo picked up a small wooden truck. "It's so smooth!" he said.

"I started making toys right here, in **Billund, Denmark**, back in **1932**," said Ole Kirk.

Juno counted the toys in a row. "One duck, two duck, three duck!"

"Ducks, trucks, and yo-yos," said Ole Kirk. "All made right in my little workshop."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well
chapters.text:
A new wooden sign leaned against the workshop wall.

Ole Kirk dipped his brush into some paint.

"What are you writing?" asked Milo.

"A new name," said Ole Kirk. "For my whole toy company."

Juno hopped closer. "Can dinosaurs help pick it?"

Ole Kirk laughed. "Not today, little one."

He painted four big letters: **L-E-G-O**.

"It comes from two Danish words," he said. " 'Leg godt.' It means 'play well.'"

Milo tried saying it slowly. "Leg-godt! Play well!"

Clack flapped his wings. "That's it exactly, Milo!"

"My company got that very name in **1934**," said Ole Kirk.

Juno clapped his hands. "Play well! Play well!"

The sign went up with a soft THUNK.

Clack spun in a happy circle. His wooden wing squeaked the whole time.

Everybody laughed at the squeak.

"Play well," Milo whispered to himself. "I like that a lot."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Hissing Machine
chapters.text:
A giant metal machine rumbled into the workshop.

It hissed like a sleepy dragon.

Milo's eyes went wide. "What IS that thing?"

"A new machine," said Ole Kirk. "It melts plastic and squirts it into shapes."

Juno sniffed the air. "It smells funny!"

"Plastic is a new kind of stuff," said Clack. "Not wood. It's smooth and hard."

Ole Kirk pulled a big lever. SPLOOSH! Melted plastic squeezed into a tiny mold.

Out popped a little plastic brick, still warm.

"In **1947**, I bought one of the very first machines like this in all of Denmark," said Ole Kirk.

Milo held the warm brick. "It's so light!"

Juno tried to stack two bricks. They wobbled. They tipped right over.

"Hmm," said Milo, tapping his chin. "These bricks need something to hold them together."

Ole Kirk nodded slowly. "You might be onto something, young man."

Juno picked the fallen bricks back up, not worried one bit.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tubes Inside
chapters.text:
A man burst into the room holding a drawing.

"Father, I think I solved it!" he said.

"This is Godtfred," said Clack. "Ole Kirk's own son."

Milo looked at the drawing. Little tubes sat inside a brick's bottom.

"What if tubes inside grabbed the bumps on top?" said Milo, pointing at the page.

Godtfred's mouth dropped open. "That's exactly my idea!"

Juno pressed two new bricks together. CLICK!

He yanked them hard. They held tight.

"IT CLICKS!" Juno shouted.

"In **1958**, this brick got its special new shape," said Godtfred. "Now towers won't fall apart."

Milo stacked ten bricks high, one careful brick at a time.

He shook the tower hard. It wiggled. It did not fall.

"Only the best is good enough. That's what I always say," said Ole Kirk, smiling at them both.

Clack clapped his wooden wings together. "Best brick ever made, if you ask me!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The First Kids to Click
chapters.text:
Clack waddled them into a sunny playroom.

Danish children sat on the floor with brick boxes.

"These kids," said Clack, "were some of the very first children ever to play with these new bricks."

A girl stacked a tall tower. A boy bumped the table by accident.

Her tower did not even wobble.

Juno gasped. "Mine always falls over!"

"Not these ones," said the girl. "Go on, try it."

Milo built a shark shape from blue bricks. Juno built a dinosaur from green ones.

They pressed their creatures nose to nose, giggling the whole time.

"Old wooden toys could crack or fall apart," said Clack. "These new bricks stick tight, every single time."

Juno stomped his brick dinosaur across the rug. CRUNCH CRUNCH CRUNCH!

Milo's brick shark did not budge, not even once.

"Play well!" all the Danish kids cheered together, waving their bricks in the air.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Whole Park Made of Bricks
chapters.text:
Big gates creaked open right in front of them.

"LEGOLAND!" read a giant painted sign.

Juno's jaw dropped open. "A whole park made of bricks?"

Brick towers, brick castles, and tiny brick boats filled the park.

A brick dinosaur stood taller than Milo, with a long brick neck.

"This park opened right in **Billund**, in **1968**," said Clack.

Milo counted little brick windows on a tiny castle. "One, two, three, four!"

Juno hugged the giant brick dinosaur's leg. "He's my friend now."

A brick shark swam slowly through a brick pond nearby.

Milo waved at it. "Hi there, shark buddy!"

Clack chuckled, waddling along beside them. "Billund is still home to the whole LEGO company, even today."

The boys ran down a brick path together, laughing the whole way down.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Little Yellow Friend
chapters.text:
A tiny yellow figure stood on the path ahead.

It had a round head and a big smiling face.

"Who's that?" asked Milo.

"A minifigure," said Clack. "That means a tiny little brick person. The very first one, from **1978**."

Juno poked its little plastic arm. It wiggled. "It moves!"

"Before this," said Clack, "LEGO people didn't have arms or legs that could bend."

Milo picked up the minifigure carefully. He moved its arm up and down.

"Now it can wave!" He waved its tiny hand at Juno.

Juno waved back, giggling so hard he snorted.

The minifigure's smile never changed, but somehow it still felt happy.

Clack nodded his wooden head. "Millions of these little folks were about to go play with kids everywhere."

Milo tucked the minifigure gently into his pocket. "I'll take good care of you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Carpet
chapters.text:
Clack tapped his wing again. WHOOOSH!

The swirly rug turned back into their own bedroom carpet.

Milo blinked. His brick tower still stood tall right beside him.

Juno hugged his toy dinosaur tight against his chest.

"Bricks made today still click with old bricks," said Clack. "The shape never ever changed."

Milo pressed a brand new brick onto an old one. CLICK! It held just perfectly.

"The LEGO company has made billions and billions of bricks," said Clack. "More than anyone could ever count."

Juno tried counting anyway. "One, two, three... a hundred!"

Everybody laughed softly in the quiet room.

Clack waddled over to the toy box and curled up small.

"Remember," he said with a sleepy quack, "play well."

A tiny wooden duck sat on the carpet, right where the glow had been.

Milo pulled his blanket over himself and over Juno too.

The toy shark and the toy dinosaur rested side by side on the shelf.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: **Ole Kirk Christiansen** was a carpenter in **Billund, Denmark**, who started making wooden toys in **1932**.
LEGO's name comes from the Danish words **"leg godt,"** which means **"play well."**
The toy company got its name **LEGO** in **1934**.
Ole Kirk carved **wooden ducks, trucks, and yo-yos** in his workshop.
In **1947**, LEGO got one of the very first machines in Denmark that could melt plastic into toy shapes.
In **1958**, the brick got little **tubes inside** that grab the bumps on the brick below, so towers hold tight.
The new **1958** bricks could be stacked into towers that do not fall apart, even when shaken.
**Godtfred**, Ole Kirk's son, helped figure out the tube shape that makes bricks click together.
The first tiny **LEGO minifigure**, with arms and legs that bend, showed up in **1978**.
Before **1978**, LEGO people could not wave or bend their arms and legs.
**Billund** is still where the whole LEGO company is based today.
**Legoland**, a whole park made of bricks, opened in **Billund** in **1968**.
Bricks made today still click perfectly with bricks made a long time ago.
The LEGO company thinks it has made **billions and billions** of bricks since it started.
